metadata.title: Willow Threshold Reconstruction — Viz Riff
metadata.purpose: Riff on the D3 surface code error rate visualization — log-log encoding, gap annotation, Lambda-to-overhead disconnection.

beats.narration_text: Bonjour, Liam — in for Bear. Claude built a quantum error correction simulator. Log-log chart, surface codes, Google Willow. We are not grading the physics. We are grading the visualization.

props.command: write me a visualization for surface code error rates
output: ✓ Willow Threshold Reconstruction — Surface Code Error Rates
✓ D3 log-log chart, three distance curves

beats.narration_text: Four panels. Main chart: logical error rate versus physical error rate, log-log. Three curves for code distances three, five, seven. Dashed vertical at the threshold at zero-point-zero-one. A red dot — Willow, zero-point-one-four-three percent. Two sliders on the right. An overhead calculator and a physics console below.

The Lambda slider drives the suppression factor. Drag it: a gap annotation line updates on the chart, connecting the d-equals-seven formula prediction to the hardcoded Willow dot. At Willow's measured Lambda of two-point-one-four, the formula gives zero-point-four-seven-seven percent; Willow measured zero-point-one-four-three. The three distance curves do not move.
beats.new_visual_element: Lambda slider sweep — gap annotation live

beats.narration_text: What it gets right: the log-log scale is doing real work. The slope of each curve is the code exponent — steeper for larger d. Below threshold, bigger code distance, exponentially lower logical error rate. The gap annotation places two exact numbers — formula prediction and Willow measured — on the same visual axis with a connecting line.
beats.new_visual_element: Still — initial state, log-log curves + gap annotation visible

beats.narration_text: Three problems. The Lambda slider and the overhead calculator are disconnected — drag Lambda, the overhead table does not follow. The Willow dot is hardcoded: it stays fixed as the formula moves, so the gap annotation spans different p-values at different Lambda settings, not just different error rates. And the y-axis label renders p underscore L in plain text while the subtitle uses HTML subscript.
beats.new_visual_element: Still — Lambda at ~3.2, overhead table unchanged from start

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Surface code suppression, visualized. The log-log encoding is correct. The gap annotation earns its place. The one fix that changes how students learn: link Lambda to the overhead panel.

artifactLines: Log-log slope encodes the exponent argument correctly
Gap annotation: two exact numbers on one visual axis
Lambda-to-overhead link is broken — one function call away from fixed
Willow dot is hardcoded — gap spans p-values, not just rates

beats.narration_text: Your turn. I built a D3 surface code error rate sim. The Lambda slider controls suppression on the main chart but does not update the overhead calculator. Fix it: when Lambda changes, auto-update p_eff into the overhead's pPhysSlider so required-d and qubit counts update live. Also: move the Willow dot with Lambda — reposition its cx to xScale of p_th divided by Lambda — so the gap annotation shows formula delta at any Lambda, not a fixed Willow baseline. Show me the updated updateLambda function with both changes.
